# Restructuring Data {#sec-restructure}

```{python}
#| include: false
import warnings
warnings.filterwarnings("ignore")
```

## Setup

Load the modules and datasets needed for the chapter.

```{python}
#| output: false
import polars as pl
from plotnine import ggplot, aes
from polars import col as c

import funs

country = pl.read_csv("data/countries.csv")
cellphone = pl.read_csv("data/countries_cellphone.csv")
```

## Introduction

@sec-collect introduced the unit of observation and the rules of tidy data, and showed that whether a table is tidy depends on the unit of observation an analysis needs. This chapter puts those ideas to work by reshaping a single table into a different layout without adding or removing information. We will see that the same set of values can be arranged in several different ways, and that picking the right arrangement, rather than the right values, is often what determines whether an analysis is easy or painful.

We will work throughout with the `cellphone` dataset, shown below. Its unit of observation is *year × country*, and in this shape it is tidy [@ch02:hadley2014tidy]: `year`, `iso`, and `cell` each get a column, and each row is one country's rate in one year.

```{python}
cellphone
```

In the next section we will pivot this table into a wide frame with one column per country, a reasonable thing to do if the analysis calls for comparing countries directly. That wide frame will be tidy for questions about a single year, and untidy the moment we want to treat country as a variable, since at that point "country" is a set of column names rather than a column. Understanding why the same set of numbers can be tidy in one shape and untidy in another is most of what you need to know to decide when a pivot is the right move.

The chapter covers pivoting and unpivoting to move between wide and long layouts, reshaping data so that it plays well with plotnine, and exploding list columns so that multiple values packed into one cell get a row each. We close by noting the one restructuring operation that does not fit this chapter's theme, because it destroys information rather than merely rearranging it.

## Pivot and Unpivot

Sometimes the unit of observation in which a data table is stored does not match the unit needed for our analysis. If the stored format uses a compound unit of observation, we can simplify it by using an aggregation to remove one or more components. For example, we could group the *plant × day* table from @sec-collect by plant ID and calculate summary statistics (such as the maximum height over all days) to generate a dataset with *plant* as the unit of observation. While aggregations are useful, by design they remove information present in the original dataset. Other times, we want to restructure the unit of observation without losing or adding any information. We simply need the data in a different shape for a particular analysis or visualization. To do this, we can use one of two additional data manipulation functions.

We could have stored the `cellphone` dataset in a format where the unit of observation was *year* and each country had its own column. What if we want to work with the data in that format? For example, if we wanted to compute the difference in cellphone ownership between the United States and Canada, we would need the data in this format. We can convert our dataset using the `.pivot()` method, which requires indicating which column will be used to index the output (this becomes the unit of observation), which column will be used to create the new columns, and which column contains the values that will fill the table.

```{python}
cell_wide = (
    cellphone
    .pivot(index=c.year, on=c.iso, values=c.cell)
)
cell_wide
```

This is the wide frame described in the introduction. It is tidy for the unit of observation *year*, and it is the layout we would want if we were computing something like the gap between two specific countries. It is not tidy for the unit of observation *year × country*, since country has moved out of the data and into the column names.

It is possible that some combinations of the new rows and columns do not exist in the original DataFrame. When this happens, Python will fill in `null` values for the missing combinations. Sometimes, particularly if these are counts that we are looking at, we may want to convert all of these missing values to zeros (or another default). To do that, we can call the method `.fill_null(0)`. The value zero can be changed to any other value that makes sense. This can also be used on individual columns as needed in other analyses.

Now, what if we want to go the other way? That is, suppose we stored the data originally in the format above (`cell_wide`) but want to return to the version we started with. This can be achieved by using the `.unpivot()` method, which requires specifying the index column to use. The new columns created to store the data are given the default names `variable` and `value`. These can be changed by setting the `variable_name` and `value_name` arguments.

```{python}
(
    cell_wide
    .unpivot(index=c.year)
)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Pivot and unpivot syntax

Polars does not itself accept the `c.` notation when specifying columns in `pivot` and `unpivot`; these two methods expect plain strings. The `funs.py` module loaded at the top of every script patches both methods so that the `c.` notation works the same way it does everywhere else, which is the form used throughout this book. If you ever call `pivot` or `unpivot` without having imported `funs`, specify the columns as strings instead: `.pivot(index="year", on="iso", values="cell")`.
:::

The `.pivot()` and `.unpivot()` methods are powerful tools for data manipulation and constitute the final major methods we need for manipulating tabular datasets. Although they may at first glance seem straightforward (and should be, at least in theory), care is needed when using them to reshape data, because they can easily introduce subtle errors. The best practice is to decide on the unit of observation up front and structure your data accordingly. Use these reshaping functions when necessary, but avoid unnecessary back-and-forth transformations that can introduce mistakes.

## Pivoting for plotnine

The tidy data framework was built with a particular use case in mind: it makes plotting predictable. plotnine expects long data, which explains several things about earlier chapters.

Try mapping a plotnine aesthetic to country using `cell_wide`. There is no `iso` column to map, only a separate column for each country, so there is no sensible way to write `color=c.iso`. Nothing in `cell_wide` tells plotnine that `USA` and `CAN` and every other column name are all values of the same underlying variable.

```{python}
#| eval: false
(
    cell_wide
    .ggplot(aes(x=c.year, y=c.USA))
    .geom_line()
)
```

This code runs, but it only gets you a single country's line, hardcoded by column name, and there is no way to extend it to "one line per country" without writing a separate `geom_line()` call for every column. Unpivoting fixes this by putting country back into the data as a variable:

```{python}
cell_long = (
    cell_wide
    .unpivot(index=c.year, variable_name=c.iso, value_name=c.cell)
)

(
    cell_long
    .filter(c.iso.is_in(["USA", "GBR", "IRL", "CAN"]))
    .ggplot(aes(x=c.year, y=c.cell, color=c.iso))
    .geom_line()
)
```

With `iso` as a column, `color=c.iso` is enough to tell plotnine to draw one line per country; here we also filter to the same four countries as in @sec-graphics, since a line per each of the 174 countries would be unreadable. This also explains why our first plot of `cellphone` by country worked with no reshaping: `cellphone` was already stored long, with one row per *year × country* combination. Before reaching for `.ggplot()`, check whether the variable you want to map to an aesthetic (color, shape, facet, and so on) has its own column. If it does not, unpivot first.

## Expand List Columns

A final type of transformation arises when multiple elements occupy a single cell in a table. This usually occurs only after a data-cleaning step we've performed, rather than as raw input from a CSV file. For example, the function `str.split` can split the text in a DataFrame column into parts. We can use this to split the multiple language codes found in the `lang` column of our data.

```{python}
(
    country
    .select(c.full_name, c.lang)
    .with_columns(
        lang_codes = c.lang.str.split("|")
    )
)
```

It is hard to work directly with the embedded list structure. Often the easiest way to simplify a data frame that contains list elements is to unravel the lists, duplicating the other columns. Use the `.explode()` method, passing the column(s) you want to unravel.

```{python}
(
    country
    .select(c.full_name, c.lang)
    .with_columns(
        lang_codes = c.lang.str.split("|")
    )
    .explode(c.lang_codes)
)
```

The term "explode" warns us that the resulting dataset can become very large, particularly if we unravel multiple columns simultaneously.

## Round Trips Versus Aggregation

Pivoting and unpivoting are round trips: pivot a long table to wide, unpivot it back, and (aside from row and column ordering) you have the original table. No values are created or destroyed, only rearranged. Aggregation is not like this. Grouping a *plant × day* table down to a *plant* table by taking the maximum height, for instance, throws away every day's measurement except the one that set the maximum, and there is no operation that gets those measurements back. Pivoting and unpivoting change a table's shape; aggregation changes its unit of observation, and it does so in one direction only. Keep the distinction in mind, since it is the reason behind the advice in @sec-collect to prefer longer formats for storing data: a long table can always be pivoted into whatever wide shape an analysis needs, but a table that has already been aggregated cannot be un-aggregated back into it.
